blocks.text: A session begins the moment a client and a server shake hands, and it keeps running for as long as that connection stays meaningful, sometimes a few seconds, sometimes an entire workday.
Everything the two sides agreed to, everything the session is watching for, and everything the conversation has covered so far all needs to live somewhere while the session is alive.
This topic opens the Context Management module by looking at that living record, called session state, and what it takes to keep it correct on both ends of the connection.
1. What a Session Actually Is
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440803447-150926192.png
A session is the stretch of time a client and a server stay connected and working together, starting at the first handshake and ending when either side disconnects.
It is not the same thing as a single request or a single tool call. A session can carry many requests, many tool calls, and many turns of conversation, all inside one ongoing relationship.
Both sides need a place to keep track of that relationship as it unfolds, and that place is what this topic calls session state.
2. What the Client Keeps Track Of

blocks.alt: What the Client Keeps Track Of
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440803733-413412188.png
The client, usually the part closest to the user, keeps its own record of the session: which server it is talking to, what that server said it could do, and what has been asked so far.
If the client loses that record, it has no way of knowing whether a resource it wants is still subscribed to, or whether a capability it is about to rely on was ever actually confirmed.

items: Which server or servers it is connected to
Capabilities the server confirmed during setup
Resources it has asked to be notified about
The conversation turns exchanged so far

blocks.text: 3. What the Server Keeps Track Of
The server keeps a mirror of much of the same information, but from its own side: which client it is serving, what it promised that client, and which resources that client is currently subscribed to.
A server that forgets its side of this record can send a notification to a client that never asked for it, or refuse a request the client believes was already approved.
Notice that this record has almost nothing to do with the words in the conversation itself. It is bookkeeping about the connection, not content for the model.
4. Negotiated Capabilities
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440803734-976882661.png
Right when a session begins, the client and server exchange a short list of what each one supports, this is called capability negotiation, and the result becomes part of session state on both sides.
Neither side should keep guessing about this later. Once negotiated, a capability is either available for the rest of the session or it is not, and both sides need to remember which.

blocks.title: Negotiate once, remember always
blocks.content: Capabilities are agreed on early in a session and then trusted for its whole lifetime. Re-checking them on every single request wastes time the negotiation step already paid for.

blocks.text: 5. Subscribed Resources
A subscription is a request to be told later if something changes, a file, a piece of data, a status value, without having to keep asking about it.

Both the client that asked for the subscription and the server that accepted it need to hold onto that fact, since the whole point of a subscription is that it outlives the single request that created it.
If either side forgets a subscription exists, a change can happen with nobody finding out, or a notification can arrive for something nobody wants anymore.
6. Conversation History So Far
As a session runs, it accumulates a conversation: what the user asked, what the assistant said, what tools were called and what they returned.
This history is one part of session state, and it is the part that tends to grow fastest, since every new turn adds to it while capabilities and subscriptions mostly stay fixed.
Keeping history as part of session state, rather than something reconstructed from scratch each time, is what lets a session feel continuous instead of forgetful.
7. A Simple Session State Object
Putting the pieces together, a session state object usually looks like a plain record with a few clearly named fields, nothing exotic.
Nothing here is complicated by itself. The difficulty shows up in deciding where this object should live, and what to do with it when the connection underneath it misbehaves.
8. In Memory State: Fast and Temporary

blocks.alt: In Memory State: Fast and Temporary
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440803734-457994688.png
The simplest place to keep session state is in memory, a plain object or variable that lives inside the running client or server process.
In memory state is fast to read and update, and for a session that starts, runs, and ends within one continuous process lifetime, it is often all that is needed.
The catch is that in memory state disappears the instant the process restarts or crashes, along with everything the session had learned up to that point.
9. When Session State Needs to Persist

Some sessions need to survive longer than a single process does, a server that restarts for a deploy, a client that closes and reopens later, a connection that needs to resume tomorrow rather than right now.
For those cases, session state needs to be written somewhere durable, a database or a file, so it can be read back after the process that first created it is gone.
Persisting state is not free. It costs time to write, and it raises new questions about what to persist and how current the saved copy needs to stay.
10. Choosing What to Keep in Memory vs What to Persist
Not every piece of session state deserves the same treatment. Some of it is only meaningful while the process is running, and some of it needs to outlive that process.

blocks.text: A good rule of thumb is that anything tied to the raw connection stays in memory, while anything tied to what the session has learned or agreed to is worth writing down.
11. What Happens When a Connection Drops

blocks.alt: What Happens When a Connection Drops
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440803734-638685486.png
A dropped connection does not, by itself, erase session state, but it does mean the transport carrying that state is gone, at least for now.

What happens next depends entirely on where the state lived. If it was only in memory and the process also went down, it is lost. If it was persisted, or the process stayed alive while just the socket dropped, it can still be recovered.
A client and server that handle this well treat a dropped connection as a pause, not necessarily as the end of the session.
12. Reconnecting: Resuming vs Starting Over
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440803735-361385529.png
When a connection comes back, the two sides have a choice, try to resume the same session where it left off, or treat the reconnect as the start of a brand new session.

Resuming means checking whether the old session state, capabilities, subscriptions, and history, is still valid and reusable. Starting over means throwing all of that away and negotiating from scratch.
Resuming is usually friendlier to the user, since it avoids repeating work and preserves context, but it only works if the saved state can be trusted.
13. Why Client and Server Can Drift Apart

blocks.alt: Why Client and Server Can Drift Apart
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440803735-590923477.png
Even without a dropped connection, a client's copy of session state and a server's copy can slowly drift apart if an update on one side is not reliably reflected on the other.
A subscription cancelled on the server but not cleared on the client is a classic example, the client keeps expecting notifications that will never arrive.
Drift like this is quiet. Nothing crashes and nothing errors, the session simply behaves as if it remembers something that is no longer true.
14. Keeping Both Sides in Sync as the Conversation Grows
As a session runs longer and its history grows, there are more moving parts that could fall out of sync, more subscriptions, more negotiated details, more turns to keep aligned.
The safest approach treats one side as the source of truth for each kind of state, usually the server for subscriptions and capabilities, and has the other side confirm rather than assume.

items: Acknowledge subscription changes explicitly instead of assuming they took effect
Send a lightweight heartbeat or state check on long running sessions
Version or timestamp session state so staleness can be detected
Prefer confirming state after a gap rather than assuming nothing changed

blocks.text: None of this needs to be elaborate. Even a simple confirmation step after any gap in communication catches most drift before it causes a real problem.
15. Session State With Multiple Clients or Servers
A single server rarely serves just one client, and a single client is often connected to more than one server at a time, which means session state cannot be one shared blob.

Each connection needs its own slice of state, keyed by session identifier, so that one client's subscriptions never leak into another client's view, and one server's capabilities never get confused with another's.

code.content:
const sessionsByClient = new Map();
// sessionsByClient.get("client-42") returns only that client's state

blocks.text: 16. Cleaning Up Session State When a Session Ends
A session that ends properly should release its subscriptions, close its connection cleanly, and let both sides drop the state that only mattered while it was active.

Skipping this step tends to pile up, subscriptions nobody is listening to anymore, in memory records for clients that left long ago, all quietly consuming memory or triggering notifications nobody wants.
Treating session end as a real event, not just a socket closing, keeps both sides tidy over the long run.
17. Designing Session State to Survive the Unexpected
A session designed well from the start treats disconnection, restart, and drift as normal events to plan for, not rare accidents.
That means separating what only matters while a connection is literally open from what matters for the life of the whole session, and being deliberate about which one gets persisted.
It also means being honest about the cost, persisting everything is safest but slowest, keeping everything in memory is fastest but fragile, and most real systems land somewhere in between.
Worked Example

A client connects to a document server and negotiates capabilities, the server supports subscriptions but not sampling. The client subscribes to a shared document and the conversation runs for twenty turns.

Midway through, the network blips and the connection drops for eight seconds. The server had persisted the subscription, and the client had checkpointed its conversation history every few turns, so reconnecting only takes one quick handshake.
The user never even notices the drop. The conversation picks up exactly where it was, and the subscription keeps delivering updates as if nothing happened.
Common Mistakes

items: Assuming session state and conversation history are the same thing
Keeping subscriptions only in memory on a server that restarts often
Never re-confirming capabilities after a reconnect
Letting a client believe a subscription is active after the server has dropped it
Persisting absolutely everything, including raw connection handles that cannot be reused anyway
Treating a dropped connection as the end of the session instead of a pause

blocks.text: Practice

Design a session state object for a client connected to a server that supports subscriptions but not sampling. Include fields for negotiated capabilities, a set of subscribed resources, and a conversation history array.
Then write a small function that decides, on reconnect, whether to resume the saved state or start a fresh session, based on how long ago the connection last dropped.
Key Takeaway

Session state is everything a client and server each keep track of for as long as a session lasts, negotiated capabilities, subscribed resources, and the conversation so far, and it needs a clear answer for what lives only in memory versus what has to be written down somewhere durable.
Handling drops, reconnects, and drift well comes down to one habit, never assume the other side remembers the same thing you do, confirm it.
